questions.subject: PHYSICS_MECHANICS
questions.topic: Kinetic energy as the work of a net force
questions.learningObjective: state what the kinetic energy of a body equals
questions.stem: A body of mass m is pushed through a distance s by a net force that varies along the way. What does the work done by that net force equal?

options.text: The change in the kinetic energy of the body, whatever the force does
The change in the momentum of the body, since force times distance is momentum
options.misconception: confuses the work done with the impulse delivered

options.text: The gain in gravitational potential energy over the same distance
options.misconception: assumes the potential energy gain is always equal to the work done

options.text: The force multiplied by the distance, since that is the definition of work
options.misconception: restates the definition without stating what the work is equal to

questions.explanation: The work done by the net force equals the change in the kinetic energy of the body, and the theorem holds however the force varies along the path, so the varying-force case needs no extra work. For a constant net force this reduces to the familiar statement that the work done equals the gain in kinetic energy, and the statement remains true when the body slows down, the work then being negative. The claim that work equals a momentum change is a category error, since force times distance has the dimensions of an energy and not of a momentum, and the potential energy gain coincides with the work only when gravity is the only force doing work.
questions.hint: Ask what quantity has the same change as the work done by the net force.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_MECHANICS
questions.topic: Conservative force and path independence
questions.learningObjective: state what makes a force conservative
questions.stem: A force acts on a body that can move between two points by many different routes. What feature of the force makes its work depend only on the endpoints?

options.text: The work in going around any closed path is zero, so the route cannot matter
The force is always at right angles to the direction of motion, so it does no work
options.misconception: confuses a conservative force with a force that does no work at all

options.text: The magnitude of the force does not change along any path, so the work is fixed
options.misconception: believes a constant magnitude is enough to fix the work

options.text: The force acts only at the start of the journey, so only the start position counts
options.misconception: believes a force applied at one point can be conservative at all

questions.explanation: A force is conservative exactly when the work it does around any closed path comes out zero, and that single condition forces the work between two points to be the same whichever route joins them, because any two routes can be turned into a closed loop. Gravity is the standard example, with its work depending only on the change in height and not on the path followed, while friction is not, since a longer zigzag route dissipates more. The two wrong answers describe forces that are not conservative for different reasons: a force at right angles to the motion does no work at all, which is a degenerate case, and a constant magnitude says nothing about the direction, which is what actually decides the work.
questions.hint: Close the path and see what the work around the loop comes to.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_MECHANICS
questions.topic: Arbitrary constant in a potential energy
questions.learningObjective: explain why only differences of potential energy are physical
questions.stem: The potential energy of a body near the ground is written as the mass times the acceleration of gravity times the height. Why can the height be measured from any convenient level?

options.text: Any constant added to the potential changes no force and no predicted motion
The zero of height can be chosen freely only when the force is conservative
options.misconception: restricts the freedom of choice to a narrower case than it applies to

options.text: The height in the formula must be measured from the ground, so it is not a choice
options.misconception: insists the zero is fixed when in fact it is a convention

options.text: Changing the zero of height changes the mass of the body, which is measured with it
options.misconception: believes the choice of zero alters a measured quantity

questions.explanation: A potential energy is defined only up to an additive constant, because the force is obtained from its negative gradient, and a constant has zero gradient and so contributes no force at all. Adding the same constant everywhere therefore changes no force, no work and no motion, and it cancels in every difference that the equations ever use. The choice of zero is a convenience that lets the numbers stay small, and it is available for every potential, conservative or not, as long as the force really does depend on position alone. The mass is a separate measured quantity and has no connection to where the height is measured from.
questions.hint: A force comes from the gradient of the potential, and a constant has no gradient.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_MECHANICS
questions.topic: Condition for mechanical energy conservation
questions.learningObjective: state the condition under which mechanical energy is conserved
questions.stem: A trolley moves along a rough track while being pushed by a motor. Which statement correctly describes the mechanical energy of the trolley?

options.text: It changes by the work done by friction and by whatever else does non-conservative work
It stays constant, because the motor replaces exactly what friction removes
options.misconception: assumes a constant total merely because the parts are being exchanged

options.text: It falls steadily, because friction is the only force acting on the trolley
options.misconception: ignores the work the motor and the trolley motor both supply

options.text: It rises without limit, because the motor keeps adding energy to the system
options.misconception: believes a motor can create energy rather than convert it from elsewhere

questions.explanation: Mechanical energy, meaning kinetic plus potential, is conserved only when every force that does work is conservative, and on a rough track with a motor running that condition plainly fails. The correct statement is the balance form: the change in mechanical energy equals the work done by the non-conservative forces, which here are friction and the motor. Friction always takes energy out while the motor puts it in, and if the two happen to match at some instant the mechanical energy is momentarily steady, but nothing guarantees that and the system is not then conservative. Total energy including the fuel and the surroundings is still conserved, which is where the motor's contribution comes from.
questions.hint: Ask which forces are doing work, and whether each of them is conservative.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_MECHANICS
questions.topic: Energy stored in a spring
questions.learningObjective: state the correct expression for the energy stored in a spring
questions.stem: A spring of stiffness k is compressed by a distance x from its natural length. Which expression gives the energy stored in it?

options.text: One half times the stiffness times the compression squared
The stiffness times the compression squared, with no factor of one half
options.misconception: drops the factor of one half that comes from the rising force

options.text: The stiffness times the compression, which is the force at that compression
options.misconception: quotes the force at the final compression as the stored energy

options.text: One half times the stiffness divided by the compression squared
options.misconception: inverts the compression, which is not how a spring stores energy

questions.explanation: The energy stored is the work done in compressing the spring, and that work is the area under the force against compression graph. Because the force rises from zero to the final value linearly, the area is a triangle, which is one half times the final force times the compression, and the final force is the stiffness times the compression, giving one half times the stiffness times the compression squared. The missing factor of one half is the single most common error in spring problems, and it always doubles the answer. The reason for it is easy to see by looking at the average force during the compression, which is only half the final force because the force was smaller all the way through.
questions.hint: The stored energy is the area under the force against compression graph, and that graph is a ramp.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_MECHANICS
questions.topic: Energy exchange in a harmonic oscillator
questions.learningObjective: describe how energy moves between the two forms in simple harmonic motion
questions.stem: A mass on a spring oscillates on a frictionless surface. Which statement describes how its energy behaves over a cycle?

options.text: Kinetic and potential energy swap, and their sum stays the same throughout
Both forms grow as the spring compresses, so the total energy increases
options.misconception: believes compression adds energy to both forms at once

options.text: Kinetic energy is largest at the turning points, where the spring is most compressed
options.misconception: locates the maximum kinetic energy at the zero-speed points

options.text: Potential energy is largest where the mass moves fastest, at the equilibrium point
options.misconception: puts the elastic energy where the speed is greatest

questions.explanation: In simple harmonic motion the two forms of energy trade places continuously, and their sum is constant because no friction is present to remove any. At the turning points the speed is zero so all the energy is potential, and at the equilibrium position the spring is at its natural length so all of it is kinetic, and everything in between is a mixture of the two. Both maxima are therefore real but they occur at opposite phases of the motion, which is exactly the kind of thing a phase diagram or an energy-versus-time graph shows at a glance. The sum being constant is what makes the total mechanical energy a useful quantity to follow, and it is available only because the surface is frictionless.
questions.hint: Follow where the speed and the compression are large at the same time.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_MECHANICS
questions.topic: Phase portrait of a harmonic oscillator
questions.learningObjective: interpret a phase portrait of an undamped oscillator
questions.stem: A phase portrait is drawn for an undamped mass on a spring, with displacement along one axis and velocity along the other. What does the resulting curve look like?

options.text: A family of nested closed ellipses, one for each value of the total energy
A single closed curve, because the total energy is fixed by the spring constant
options.misconception: believes the spring constant alone fixes the amplitude of every orbit

options.text: A set of parallel straight lines whose slope is the ratio of mass to stiffness
options.misconception: confuses a trajectory in position and velocity with a linear velocity law

options.text: A spiral moving outward until the motion stops, even with no damping present
options.misconception: describes a damped trajectory for a system that has no damping

questions.explanation: Conservation of energy ties the displacement and the velocity together at every instant, and writing the total energy as one half times the mass times the velocity squared plus one half times the stiffness times the displacement squared equal to a constant defines an ellipse in that plane. Each value of the total energy gives a different ellipse, so the undamped motion fills the plane with nested closed curves, and the system can never cross from one to another because that would change the energy. Larger ellipses mean larger amplitudes, and the two semi-axes of a given ellipse are the amplitude and the maximum speed, which is why the two forms of energy can be read straight off the picture.
questions.hint: Write the energy conservation condition as an equation relating velocity and displacement.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_MECHANICS
questions.topic: Advantage of the impulse-momentum route
questions.learningObjective: explain when the impulse-momentum route is easier than an energy route
questions.stem: A bullet passes through a block of wood that is free to slide on a frictionless floor. Why is the impulse-momentum relation usually the easier route here?

options.text: The force and the contact time are both unknown, but their product is what momentum needs
Kinetic energy cannot be used at all when a body passes through another body
options.misconception: believes energy accounting is unavailable in an interaction like this

options.text: Momentum conservation does not require knowing how much energy the block absorbs
options.misconception: confuses an advantage of the route with a claim that energy is irrelevant

options.text: The block's speed after the bullet leaves is too small for an energy calculation
options.misconception: believes small numbers are a reason to avoid an energy approach

questions.explanation: The energy route needs the work done on the block, and that work requires knowing how far the block moves during the contact, which is not known and would have to be found by a simultaneous calculation. The momentum route needs only the product of the contact force and the contact time, and neither factor has to be known, because the impulse is exactly what conservation of momentum supplies for the pair. That is why bullet and block problems, explosions and recoil events are standard applications of impulse and momentum. Energy is not unavailable in such an event, it simply cannot be found without extra information about the internal motion, and it then serves as a way to check the answer.
questions.hint: Ask which quantity each route needs the unknown contact details for.

questions.topic: Speed found from the work done by a net force
questions.learningObjective: find a speed from the work done by a net force
questions.stem: A constant net force of 3.00 N acts on a 0.500 kg body that starts from rest, and it moves 4.00 m in the direction of the force. What speed does the body reach, in metres per second?
questions.explanation: The work done by the net force is the force times the distance, which is 3.00 times 4.00, giving 12.0 J, and that equals the gain in kinetic energy, so the speed satisfies one half times 0.500 times the speed squared equal to 12.0, which gives a speed of 6.93 m/s. Working through the acceleration instead, the net force divided by the mass is 6.00 m per second squared, and the standard speed relation for constant acceleration gives the speed as the square root of twice 6.00 times 4.00, which is again 6.93 m/s. The energy route is preferable when the force varies, since the speed-squared relation then does not apply but the work integral still does.
questions.hint: Equate the work done by the net force to the gain in kinetic energy.

questions.topic: Distance needed to stop against friction
questions.learningObjective: find the stopping distance of a body sliding against friction
questions.stem: A 2.00 kg trolley slides along a level floor with a coefficient of friction of 0.250 and an initial speed of 8.00 m/s. Take g as 9.80 m/s per second squared. How far does it travel before stopping, in metres?
questions.explanation: The kinetic energy at the start is one half times 2.00 times 64.0, which is 64.0 J, and the friction force is the coefficient times the weight, which is 0.250 times 2.00 times 9.80, or 4.90 N, so the distance needed to use up that energy is 64.0 divided by 4.90, giving 13.06 m. The kinematics route agrees, since the deceleration is the friction divided by the mass, 2.45 m per second squared, and the distance from the speed-squared relation is 64.0 over twice 2.45, again 13.06 m. The important feature is the inverse square: doubling the speed quadruples the stopping distance, which is why a modest gain in speed buys a great deal of extra stopping room.
questions.hint: All the initial kinetic energy goes into the work of friction over the stopping distance.

questions.topic: Energy dissipated by friction on a slope
questions.learningObjective: compute the energy lost to friction on a downward slide
questions.stem: A 3.00 kg block slides 6.00 m down a slope inclined at 30.0 degrees to the horizontal, starting from rest, with a coefficient of friction of 0.200. Take g as 9.80 m/s per second squared. How much mechanical energy is dissipated by friction during the slide, in joules?
questions.explanation: The friction force is the coefficient times the component of the weight pressing into the slope, which is 0.200 times 3.00 times 9.80 times the cosine of 30.0 degrees, giving 5.092 N, and the work it does over 6.00 m is 30.55 J. questions.stem: A 0.010 kg bullet passes through a 2.00 kg block of wood that is free to slide on a frictionless floor, entering at 500 m/s and leaving at 300 m/s. What speed does the block move off at, in metres per second?

questions.topic: Centre-of-mass speed of a two-body system

questions.stem: A 3.00 kg body moves at 6.00 m/s to the right and a 1.00 kg body is at rest, and nothing external acts on the pair. What is the speed of the centre of mass of the two bodies, in metres per second?

questions.topic: Rocket speed change set by the mass ratio
questions.learningObjective: explain what determines the speed change a rocket achieves
questions.stem: Two rockets have the same exhaust speed. The first starts at 2000 kg and the second at 5000 kg, and both end at 500 kg. Which statement about their speed changes is correct?

options.text: The second gains more, because its mass ratio of 10 is larger than the first's 4
The first gains more, because a smaller rocket is easier to accelerate from rest
options.misconception: confuses a fixed thrust acting on a smaller mass with a larger mass ratio

options.text: Both gain the same, because their exhaust speeds are identical
options.misconception: believes the exhaust speed alone fixes the speed change

options.text: The second gains less, because its extra 3000 kg must also be accelerated

options.misconception: reads the quality factor as a count of oscillations to rest

Nor is it a frequency ratio, because at resonance the driving frequency and the natural frequency agree to within a small fraction, so that ratio is always close to one and carries little information.

answer.exemplar: Start from the work-energy theorem, which says the work done by the net force equals the change in kinetic energy, and split that net force into a conservative part and a non-conservative part. The work of the conservative part is minus the change in its potential energy, since a conservative force is defined as one whose work depends only on the endpoints and equals the negative of the potential energy change, so moving that term to the other side gives the change in kinetic plus potential energy equals the work of the non-conservative forces. That rearranged form is exactly the energy conservation statement, and the rearrangement is reversible, so neither is more fundamental than the other. The difference is only in what each is good for. The work-energy form is the better one when the net force is known as a function of position and the speed is wanted, since it needs no potential at all; for a 0.500 kg body pulled 4.00 m by a net force of 3.00 N from rest it gives a speed of 6.93 metres per second in one step. The conservation form is better when the system has to be tracked through several stages or when a potential is already known, since it needs only endpoint values and makes the final state computable without following the motion.

questions.explanation: A stem of this kind should be answered by doing the rearrangement rather than by asserting a connection, so the exemplar splits the net force, moves the conservative term across, and shows that the two statements are the same equation read in two places. It then has to name a case for each version, because the practical difference between them is what makes the item worth asking, and a worked number for the work-energy route is the quickest way to make that concrete.

answer.exemplar: The difference is what is known at each stage. During the impact the internal forces between the two cars are equal and opposite and act for the same time on each, so they cancel in the total momentum of the pair, and with no significant external impulse the total momentum is unchanged. Nothing about how the cars deform is needed for that statement. Energy is different, because the work done on a car during the impact is the contact force multiplied by the distance it moves while being crushed, and neither the force history nor the crush distance is known, so the energy route is simply unavailable at that moment. After the cars have separated, the situation reverses: momentum is no longer conserved, because friction on the road is an external force, while the mechanical energy does stay constant on a level road because friction is the only force doing work and it is conservative on a straight horizontal surface, and the kinetic energy at the start of the slide is then measured by the stopping distance. Putting the two together turns momentum into an energy statement, since the kinetic energy immediately after the impact equals the work done by friction during the slide, and the difference between the kinetic energy the cars had before the impact and that value is exactly the energy that went into deformation, heating and sound.

questions.explanation: The argument has to be organised around which forces are external and which internal at each stage, since that is what decides the validity of each law, and the exemplar keeps the impact and the slide separate for exactly that reason. questions.topic: A speed claim that energy accounting contradicts
questions.learningObjective: evaluate a measured speed against the energy budget of a slide
questions.stem: A 2.00 kg trolley is released from rest at a height of 2.00 m and is measured to reach 6.00 m per second at the bottom of the slope. A report claims the slope is frictionless. Take g as 9.80 m/s per second squared. Explain what the energy accounting says and what the measurement implies.

answer.exemplar: A frictionless slope has a completely determined outcome, so the claim can simply be tested against it. The potential energy released is the mass times the gravity times the height, which is 2.00 times 9.80 times 2.00, giving 39.2 J, and a frictionless slide converts all of that into kinetic energy, so the speed at the bottom would be the square root of twice 39.2 divided by 2.00, which is 6.261 metres per second. The measured value of 6.00 metres per second is smaller than that, so the report's claim cannot be right, and the shortfall is real energy removed rather than a measurement subtlety. Working out the kinetic energy actually delivered, one half times 2.00 times 36.0, which is 36.0 J, leaves 39.2 minus 36.0, that is 3.20 J, dissipated on the way down. A speed larger than 6.261 metres per second would have been the more alarming possibility, because no amount of friction can produce it, and a body gaining energy on a bare slope would mean something else was pushing it.

questions.explanation: A falsifiable claim like this one has to be tested against the single value a frictionless slide permits, so the exemplar computes that value first and then compares, which settles the question in one line. The energy shortfall has to be quantified rather than merely noted, and the final sentence is needed because the stem asks for both directions of failure, so a reader should know which of the two possible errors is the more alarming one and why friction can never produce it.
questions.hint: Compare the measured speed with the speed a frictionless slide of the same height must give.
